image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Circular hierarchical **treemap / Voronoi treemap**.

2. **Layout techniques**:
- **Hierarchical nesting**: Large regions contain smaller subregions.
- **Partitioned by category**: The circle is split into two top-level groups.
- **Area encoding**: Region size represents amount.
- **Color grouping**: Two colors distinguish the two top-level plans.
- No axes, no faceting, no stacking.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Plan (Infrastructure plan, Families plan) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue; top-level grouped region within the circle; legend |
| Major spending category (e.g., Transportation, Buildings and Utilities, In-Home Care, Jobs and Innovation, Tax Credits, Child and Family Support, Education, I.R.S.) | Categorical/nominal | Nested region/grouping; text label |
| Program / line item within category (e.g., Roads and bridges, Affordable housing, Child care, Pell grants, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Individual polygon region; text label |
| Amount ($ billions / trillions) | Quantitative | Area/size of regions; numeric text labels inside regions; totals in legend |

Visible note:
- Units are stated as **amounts on the chart in billions**, while top-level legend totals are shown in **trillions**.

comments.raw_comment:
“President Biden’s New Plan For The Future”

After analyzing the graph we noticed that The $4.1 trillion plan is split into two categories: infrastructure plan and families plan. Also, some of the categories are only split into two subcategories like tax credits, but other categories have many subcategories like jobs and innovation. The category with the most spending is in tax credits: expansion of child earned income and child dependent care tax credits. We had some questions about the graph such as is President Biden’s plan completely finalized, or will change in the future? Why is more money spent on free universal preschool rather than two years free of community college?  We also wonder why a small amount of money is being spent on teachers as they are very important to our society. We also wonder how the public will take President Biden’s plan and why the graph wasn’t split into a pie chart instead of two halves of a circle. This impacts our community because what the money is being spent on impacts everyone in different ways in our everyday lives. As students who are going into college, 2 years of free community college is a lot of saved money.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the two parts of President Biden’s economic plan:  $2.3 trillion Infrastructure Plan and $1.8 trillion Families Plan.  The diagram shows the President’s allocation of the $4.1 trillion of new spending and tax cuts to 50 programs.   The infrastructure plan would involve 8 years of spending paid for with 15 years of higher corporate taxes.  The Families Plan would cover over 10 years of spending and taxes on the wealthiest Americans.   To add some  perspective on these very large numbers, the 2020 annual U.S. Gross Domestic Product, a measure of the size of the economy, was $21.4 trillion. The recently released 2020 U.S. Census found 331 million people. 

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graphic and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

This is the last “What’s Going On In This Graph?” release of the school year.  We will return in early September.  Subscribe to the free NYT Learning Network newsletter to be notified of the next school year’s first release. 

Keep noticing and wondering.

Sure, the benefits of preschool become negligible later on, but college is almost always required for a good paying job. I also wonder why there is more money put into incentives for electric vehicles than clean energy, as its been shown that power plants are among the largest source of pollution. I think all of these ideas will be impactful in their own way, but one that I think will have a significant impact if more money being put into railways. This will likely improve the train station, and I think that will help the United States in many diverse and useful ways. This graph is showing some budget plans. I think it should be called, " Biden's Budget Burgers".

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed in the graph was the size of each category and how there were four categories for both the infrastructure and family plan. Additionally, some of the categories include many smaller sub-divisions (such as the jobs and innovation category), though others don't include anything other than the plan itself (such as In-Home Care). What was even more suprising, in my opinion, was how close in size each section was, which shows that this plan is virtually divided equally. However, sub-divisions inside each category are not as equally distributed, such as in education. This category impacts me the most, as I am still a student going through the education system. Funding for schools, and other education related purposes, are so important to balance out because the education system has been lacking some attention these past fews year, particularly in Arizona. I find it very interesting that the ratio between the funding for teaching and the plan for preschools is about 1:22. That's quite surprising considering that teachers are needed for education to happen, and preschool does not need as much to function as an organization (not everyone goes to preschool even when it's free, less trips/extracurriculars than a primary/secondary school and generally less neccessary supplies). Lastly, I would like to mention that a potential title for this graph could be "U.S. Government Spending Plan." Very straight-forward and blunt, but it gets to the point.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed when looking at the graph was the overwhelming amount of detail included in the infrastructure plan compared to the family plan. The infrastructure plan is divided into far more specific ideas. While the family plan seems far more generalized. However, what Biden plans to do with the infrastructure money is absolutely important. I agree with the attention to environmental solutions as well as a goal in an uptick in living standards. I wonder how the plan will be received by Wahington and how the plan will be executed. The plan is received well I could expect nothing less than what is portrayed on the graph. This has a direct impact on me and my community as well as every other community in the United States. For communities such as Reading, if the plan was followed through with the teachers and students of Reading would have visible growth in their education standards. A graph such as this is one that to me seems scary to put out as the President of the United States. A graph that is filled with so much hope and good things is often perceived as a promise rather than an idea. That being said if I were to write a headline for this graph I would have it say something like, "Biden's promise" Something to catch the people's attention.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that the graph shows that President Biden plans to spend a half trillion more dollars on his infrastructure plan which is split into the broad categories: buildings and utilities, transportation, jobs and innovation, and in-home care. This makes me wonder if President Biden values infrastructure more in order to fix what he thinks is wrong with the United States economy. However, this graph also shows that he acknowledges that the American families need help because of his families plan. Therefore, this graph allows people to see that President Biden cares equally about the issues presented in his plans because the graph is almost split in half money wise. When this money is set aside for families, quality of life will improve for most people because they will have better access to schooling. Crime may also decline because families will gain financial support and become less desperate to obtain money. With more money funding transportation, the effects of climate change will slow because more people will have access to public transit and zero-emission cars. In the end, this graph needs a name. I dub thee: "Hope for a Better America"

1. I noticed that most of Biden's money is going towards his infrastructure plan. Biden is extremely specific with where he's going to spend his money.

2. I'm wondering how effective his plan will be. Essentially, I'm wondering if the infrastructure plan is backed up by evidence from local communities, etc. Is Biden forwarding the right amount of money to specific places that need it? What more can he do?

comments.raw_comment:
1. When analyzing the graph, I initially noticed the split between orange and green. When looking closer, it became apparent that each side represents a different part of Biden's $4.1 trillion infrastructure and families plan; orange for infrastructure and green for families. Each main colored category is again divided, and those divisions are divided again into more specific sections and marked with prices. Interestingly, In-Home Care and I.R.S. are the only divisions within the colored split not divided again, and there is one for each side of the split. 
2. As seen below the graph, Biden plans to pay for the plan using increased tax from corporations and the wealthiest Americans. I wonder how these people are currently reacting to the idea proposed and (if it is activated) how they will react later. What problems might spring from their willingness or unwillingness to pay?
3. Having less expensive community colleges could seriously benefit youth today. Particularly those in low-income families by making a higher level education available. Not yet exposed to the adult world, the effects the plan currently has on me are low. But later in life, the effects of this plan could impact my future. Certain parts of the infrastructure receiving more money will provide better job opportunities in those divisions. 
4. We a clear demonstration showing where the money in Biden's plan is going. Title:  President Biden's $4.1 Trillion plan.

This graph has an abundant amount of information but what I noticed immediately was that a little more than half of the graph is red while the other is green. By the looks of it, President Biden plans on working mostly on the infrastructure and families of the country. To be more specific, he plans on working on buildings and utilities the most in infrastructure along with transportation, jobs and innovations, and in-home care. On the topic of families, it seems he wants to help with tax credits, child and family support, education, and a little on the IRS. I also notice that within each section there are small pieces with exactly what he is focusing on and how much money he wants to put in each topic. I wonder how long it might take for both plans to be completed and how the society might change or improve once they are complete. Based on what is on the graph it seems that my community and I will be affected positively. It looks like these ideas may really help us. 

"Is this the future?"

The thing I notice right away is that the chart seems to be attempting to be a pie chart but falls a little short in the actual presentation of the chart. I also notice that infrastructure has more tiny pieces whereas the family section has larger pieces.
I wonder how each section was decided. I think putting together a budget, especially one of this size, is extremely difficult so I wonder how each amount of money was divided up so that the needs of each section would be met. I also wonder how different age groups will react to this budgeting. I know people that are younger, millennials and gen z, have been pushing for a lot of this green energy and free education stuff. It makes me think how older generations might feel, possibly seeing this as another way younger people have it easy. 
I think a lot of this will affect everyone in the US. As someone currently in community college I know this would benefit a lot of my friends and peers who struggle financially. I also know that affordable housing is extremely important as the cost of living is on the rise. Looking at my situation currently, I won't be able to leave home until my early 20s, something past generations didn't do.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the Infrastructure Plan budget is larger than the Families Plan budget, by about 0.5 trillion, which is quite a significant amount. I think it’s important that the money is coming straight from citizens’ taxes and technically, we are the ones that are funding this plan. 

I wonder if this is a direct reflection of what the Biden administration is prioritizing right now, infrastructure over families. I’m not exactly sure how urgent the need for improved infrastructure is right now in the country, but I’m sure that there will be questions about if this is the best use of the country’s budget and if that’s more important than the issue of local economies with the pandemic. 

I’m not sure how much effect the Infrastructure Plan will have on small towns like ours. I think that it will be mainly focused on bigger commercial cities. So, I don’t think the Infrastructure Plan will affect me, personally, that much. On the other hand, the Families Plan has a large percentage dedicated to education, and as a highschool student, that is bound to have visible impacts on the environments that I spend much of my time in. Whether that ends up making school cheaper overall, I don’t know. 

The graph is split up into two sections, the Infrastructure Plan and the Families Plan. Each of these sections are then further divided into smaller categories like Buildings and Utilities, Transportation, Child and Family Support, etc. 
Title: “Get in Loser, we’re going Shopping”
